projects.name: Vestige Engine
projects.tagline: A 3D game engine built from scratch.
projects.blurb: A modern 3D game engine written in C++ from the ground up — ray-traced rendering, dynamic lighting, physics, animation, audio and scripting, all driven by a modular engine loop. Built-in profiling and editor tools round it out.

projects.name: Ants Terminal
projects.tagline: A fast, modern terminal tuned for smoother coding sessions.
projects.blurb: A lightweight Qt6 terminal for Linux, built from scratch. Its standout feature is deep, fully-local integration with Claude Code to make AI-assisted development sessions faster and leaner — nothing is sent anywhere it doesn't need to be.

screenshots.alt: Ants Terminal running a live Claude Code session over a dark theme, with a row of per-project tabs and an assistant working through a task
The built-in Roadmap dialog for a project — filterable, card-based roadmap items grouped by status, with search and kind filters
The Review Changes dialog showing a project's git status and unpushed commits, with Refresh and Copy Diff buttons
Ants Terminal in a different colour theme, displaying a detailed multi-thread stack trace from a crash report

video.caption: A silent 25-second clip of Ants Terminal in its dark theme. It opens on a plain prompt, moves into its own source folder and clears the screen, then lists the first twenty source files. Finally it prints the words 'colour and Unicode' in green, blue and magenta, followed by a tick, a lambda and a sparkle. Recorded with demoreel.

projects.name: RetroDB
projects.tagline: A ROM library manager for 150+ retro gaming systems.
projects.blurb: A web-based collection manager for retro games across 150+ platforms: hybrid metadata scraping, achievements and trophy integration, ROM tools (CHD conversion, duplicate finding, multi-disc handling), an analytics dashboard, multiple themes and role-based multi-user access.

screenshots.alt: The RetroDB library page in its dark neon theme, filled with invented games: a sidebar menu on the left, a big glowing "All Games" heading reading "39 games across all systems", a search box with system and type dropdowns, filter buttons for genre, series, publisher, developer, players, perspective, dimension, rating, source, achievements and bonus discs, an A-to-Z jump bar, and the first game card, "Aqua Rampart" for the Sega Mega Drive, showing its red cover art, genre, developer, publisher, year, age-rating badges, an "In Progress" status and two review scores.

One game's page, "Paper Planet" for the Sony PlayStation, with a blurred moonlit backdrop behind a row of Play, Clear, Edit, Scrape and Delete buttons, a blue cover picture, tags for the year 1997, 4 players, the Europe region and two scores, a play-status dropdown set to "Not Started", a one-line description, the publisher, developer and genre, Teen and PEGI 12 age-rating badges, and a strip of three pixel-art gameplay screenshots underneath.

The "Gaming Systems" page with a "5 consoles detected" badge, a search box and type and feature filters, and a grid of console cards: the Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Advance in full view with their logos, 7 games each, a console or handheld tag and a RetroAchievements tag, and the Sega Mega Drive and PlayStation cards starting below.

The dashboard, with tabs for Overview, Systems, Playing, Added and Status, "Random Game" and "Scan Library" buttons, a "Collection Health" panel showing 100% overall, with smaller rings at 100% for box art and descriptions and 0% for achievements, and summary tiles for 5 systems, 39 games, 0 missing metadata and 39 complete.

projects.name: MAME Curator
projects.tagline: Picks the best playable arcade games from a MAME set.
projects.blurb: Turns a 40,000-machine MAME set into a human-sized arcade library. It intelligently chooses the best version of each game, lets you override picks in a browser UI, copies the chosen ROMs plus required BIOSes, and writes a ready-to-use RetroArch playlist.

projects.name: Perch
projects.tagline: Remembers every window's size and spot, with snap layouts.
projects.blurb: A system-tray window manager that remembers where each window lives — position, size, monitor and virtual desktop — and restores it on reopen. Snap presets, named layouts, per-monitor profiles, a rules engine and global hotkeys, with backends for X11 and KWin/Wayland.

screenshots.alt: Perch's settings window on its Layouts page. A layout named "coding" is selected, described as "Editor left, browser right", and has two entries: the code editor takes 60% of the primary screen's width on the left, and Firefox the remaining 40% on the right.

Perch's Rules page, noting that rules are checked from top to bottom and the first match wins. A table lists three example rules: one maximises the browser, one sizes the terminal to half the screen's width and height, and one sends the music player to virtual desktop 2.

Perch's General settings page. Checkboxes to start Perch at login and to restore each window's remembered position when it reopens are ticked; showing a notification on restore is not. Below are a theme choice, set to light, and a button to run the setup wizard again. A sidebar on the left lists the other pages: Windows, Rules, Layouts, Profiles, Hotkeys, Exclusions and Import / Export.

projects.name: RetroArch
projects.tagline: My fork of the reference frontend for 100+ emulator cores.
projects.blurb: RetroArch is the de-facto frontend for the libretro API, supporting 100+ emulator and game-engine cores across a huge range of platforms. This is my personal fork tracking the upstream libretro/RetroArch project with my own changes on top.

screenshots.alt: RetroArch's Ozone menu in dark grey. A sidebar on the left lists Main Menu, Settings, History, Favorites, Images, Import Content, Contentless Cores and Explore. The main panel lists Load Core (highlighted), Load Content, Playlists, Netplay, Online Updater, Information and Configuration File, each with a one-line description underneath.

RetroArch's XMB menu: a row of category icons runs across a flowing blue wave background, in the style of a games-console home screen. Below it is a vertical list starting with Load Core, then Load Content, Playlists, Netplay, Online Updater, Information, Configuration File, Show Desktop Menu, Restart and Quit.

RetroArch's RGUI menu, a retro text-only style: green and white pixel lettering on a dark checkered background inside a green border. It lists the main menu options with an arrow pointing at Load Core, and "Select which core to use." along the bottom.

projects.name: Album Builder
projects.tagline: Curate albums from recordings, with lyric-sync and reports.
projects.blurb: A desktop tool for shaping albums out of a folder of recordings: per-track curation, drag-to-reorder, live preview with optional lyric syncing, cross-album reuse tracking, and export to M3U playlists, numbered folders and polished PDF/HTML reports.

screenshots.alt: Album Builder's main screen in a dark theme, with an invented library: a song library list on the left with the song "Lanterns on the Water" highlighted, the track order for a draft album called "Night Drive" in the middle, and on the right the song now playing with its colourful fractal cover art, title, album and artist, above playback controls.

Album Builder's player tab in a dark theme: large fractal cover art for the song "Paper Boats" by Harbour Lights, with playback controls and a progress bar below it, and an "Up Next" queue on the right listing the playing song.

projects.name: Snatch
projects.tagline: A friendly desktop frontend for yt-dlp.
projects.blurb: A graphical front-end for yt-dlp with four tabs: download (paste or drag a URL, queue many), search (with preview), media info (inspect local files), and history. Cookie import for age-gated videos, SponsorBlock, subtitles, audio merging and one-click self-update.

screenshots.alt: Snatch's Download tab with Big Buck Bunny loaded (© Blender Foundation, CC-BY 3.0): a thumbnail of the giant rabbit beside its title and running time, and below it a table of the 47 available formats, listing audio-only and video streams by type, resolution, size and codec, with buttons to pick the best video, the best MP4 or audio only.

The Search tab after searching Blender Studio's own channel for "open movie": a numbered list of results such as Spring, CHARGE and Coffee Run, each with its channel, running time and view count, above a built-in video player area.

The History tab listing four past downloads, Big Buck Bunny, Sintel, Elephants Dream and Tears of Steel, with the date, the format such as MP4 1080p or MP3 audio, and where each file was saved, plus buttons to open the file or its folder.

projects.name: Games Hub
projects.tagline: Fourteen desktop games in one small window.
projects.blurb: Chess, Draughts, Reversi, Minesweeper, Sudoku, Snake, 2048, Pinball, Hearts, Canasta and four kinds of patience — Klondike, Spider, FreeCell and Pyramid — in a single Qt 6 window sized to sit beside whatever you are actually working on. The board games play against the computer at three strengths. Nothing to install: each download carries its own copy of Qt, so it runs on a machine that has never had it.

screenshots.alt: The Games Hub start screen, headed "Pick a game", showing large dark tiles in rows of three, each with a picture and a name: Chess, Reversi, Draughts, Minesweeper, Solitaire, Spider, FreeCell, Pyramid and Sudoku, with more below.
A new game of Klondike solitaire on a green table, with the draw pile top left, four empty ace spaces top right, and seven columns of large, clearly printed cards below.
A chess board at the start of a game, cream and green squares with the pieces in their starting positions, labelled a to h and 1 to 8, with Easy, Medium and Hard difficulty buttons in the toolbar.

A four-player Canasta game in progress on a deep red table, with the player's hand of large cards at the bottom, both teams' melds laid out in the middle, the stock and discard pile in the centre, and the two team scores in the top corners.

projects.name: DOOM Ants
projects.tagline: A ray-traced reimagining of id's DOOM on modern Linux.
projects.blurb: A two-stage modernisation of the 1997 DOOM source: first bringing the ancient code to SDL2 on 64-bit Linux, then evolving the renderer toward true 3D with hardware ray tracing, dynamic lighting and volumetric effects — while keeping the original's feel. Early days.

screenshots.alt: The classic DOOM title screen with the New Game menu, rendered by DOOM Ants
Classic DOOM gameplay in a widescreen view — a marine facing a computer-room level over a blue floor
The same DOOM level with hardware ray tracing — realistic shadows and dynamic lighting darkening the room

projects.name: UT Ants
projects.tagline: Plays your Unreal Tournament maps on a modern engine.
projects.blurb: Unreal Tournament is from 1999 and people are still playing it and still making maps for it — one Monster Hunt server here carries 515 of them. The engine underneath is frozen: shadows are painted into the walls at build time, and the computer players walk into a closed door and stop. UT Ants is a new engine that reads the maps you already have and rebuilds each one as a modernised version of itself — moving shadows, real materials, fog and light shafts — while running, dodging and shock-combos feel exactly as your hands expect. It ships none of Epic's content: you bring your own copy of the game. Very early, and there is nothing to download yet.

projects.name: Slipcase
projects.tagline: Turns flat 2D game covers into realistic 3D box renders.
projects.blurb: A desktop tool that turns a flat 2D cover image into a photorealistic 3D box render — front, spine, top edge and a soft shadow, at the real millimetre measurements of fifteen case types from NES cartridge boxes to Switch cases. It can find the artwork for you, invent a spine when your cover has none, do a whole folder at once, and spin the box as an animation. Output is transparent PNG sized for RetroArch or LaunchBox. It runs, and there is no packaged download yet — for now you run it from a copy of the source.

projects.name: Contact List
projects.tagline: A secure contact manager with Google Contacts sync.
projects.blurb: A desktop contact manager for people and companies: search, custom fields, and two-way sync with Google Contacts, built with a security-first design.

screenshots.alt: The main contact list, with invented contacts, headed "15 contacts": the first five are in view, with coloured initial avatars, star marks on three favourites, and each contact's email and phone number, under a search box, an A-to-Z letter bar and a row of tag filters such as family, friends and work.

One contact's page for Amara Okafor, a starred individual, showing her email, phone number, a note that reads "Met at the community garden", her birthday, and the tags friends and garden, with Edit, Delete and Back buttons below.
The Upcoming Birthdays page listing five contacts whose birthdays fall in the next 30 days, each with the date, the age they will turn, and how many days away it is, from 2 days to 23 days.
The empty New Contact form, with fields for type, name, email, phone, a photo upload, notes and tags.

projects.name: Rolodex
projects.tagline: An encrypted credential vault with auto-masking.
projects.blurb: A GTK4 credential manager that keeps your logins in an encrypted vault (Fernet + PBKDF2), with automatic masking of sensitive fields and a fast, low-friction search.

projects.name: Rusty PSN
projects.tagline: Download PS3 & PS4 game updates straight from Sony.
projects.blurb: A Rust tool that fetches PS3 and PS4 game updates directly from Sony's servers, with both a graphical app and a command-line interface. My fork of RainbowCookie32's rusty-psn.

projects.name: finbreak
projects.tagline: Breaks your finances into categories — private and offline.
projects.blurb: A private, offline desktop app that breaks personal finances down into income and expenditure categories across multiple accounts — with charts, trends, automatic transfer detection, and password-protected PDF reports. Your data never leaves your machine.

video.caption: A silent 32-second tour of finbreak, in dark theme, using invented demo data. It opens on the lock screen, where the master password is typed. The Home dashboard follows for August — 'August looked like a normal month', net R 10,533.21 — where three donut charts break down spending by category, income by source and transfers between accounts. It then moves through Transactions (306 rows sorted into categories such as Groceries, Fuel and Dining out), the Categories tree, Recurring (suggested payments above confirmed ones), Accounts and Transfers, before returning to the dashboard. Recorded with demoreel.

screenshots.alt: The finbreak dashboard in dark theme with 'Previous month' selected and a net of R 10,533.21. Three donut charts across the top break down spending by category, income by source (Salary, Interest) and transfers (Cheque account to Savings). Below, panels list Spending R 21,551.79 (Rent/Mortgage R 9,500, Groceries R 3,524.50, Transport R 3,012.45 and more), Income R 32,085.00 and Transfers R 3,000.00, with a monthly recurring summary and an income-versus-spending bar chart along the bottom.

The Transactions view in light theme: a searchable, sortable table of 306 transactions with Date, Amount, Currency, Description, Account and Category columns. Rows show South African merchants such as Shell, Pick n Pay, Ocean Basket, Bolt, KFC and Checkers automatically sorted into categories like Fuel, Groceries, Dining out and Ride-hailing, with income amounts in green and expenses in red.

The Categories screen in dark theme showing the category tree. Expenditure branches into Bills & utilities (Electricity, Internet, Mobile), Entertainment (Dining out, Streaming), Groceries, Transport (Fuel, Ride-hailing) and more; Income branches into Gifts, Interest, Salary and Sales. Fields at the bottom let you add a category, move it under a parent, or delete the selected one.

The Recurring view in light theme with two tables. 'Suggested recurring items' lists payments finbreak has auto-detected — Outsurance, FNB Credit, Dis-Chem and City of Cape Town — awaiting Confirm or Dismiss. 'Confirmed recurring items' lists Vodacom, Spotify, Netflix, DStv, Afrihost Fibre and an Acme salary, each with its direction, monthly cadence, amount and next due date.

The Rules screen in light theme: a table of auto-categorisation rules mapping a text pattern to a category — nando to Fast food, vodacom to Mobile, netflix to Streaming, uber to Ride-hailing, engen to Fuel, and checkers and woolworths to Groceries. Buttons let you Add, Edit, Delete or reorder rules and apply them to existing transactions.

The Transfers view in dark theme showing automatic transfer detection. An empty 'Suggested transfers' pane sits above 'Confirmed transfers', a list of monthly R 3,000 movements from the Cheque account to Savings dating back through 2025, each with a date, amount and description. finbreak pairs these so a transfer is not double-counted as both income and expense.

projects.name: OneUp
projects.tagline: One-click openSUSE updates from a single window.
projects.blurb: A no-nonsense update dashboard for openSUSE (Tumbleweed and Leap) that runs the four updates you actually need — system packages, Flatpaks, firmware and leftover-package cleanup — the correct way, from one window. Each task is a toggle; check for updates read-only, roll back to a pre-update snapshot in one click, and let it check weekly in the background. It never runs as root — privileged work goes through your desktop's standard password prompt.

screenshots.alt: The OneUp dashboard in dark theme: five toggle cards — System packages (12 available), Flatpak apps (3 available), Firmware (up to date), Leftover packages and Package cache — each with a green on-switch, above Check for updates and Run selected updates buttons and a live log reading '15 update(s) available'
The same OneUp update dashboard in light theme, showing it follows the desktop's light/dark setting — identical toggle cards, buttons and read-only check log on a white background

projects.name: LottoTracker
projects.tagline: Catches the lottery win sitting unnoticed in your inbox.
projects.blurb: Reads the lottery ticket confirmations your bank sends by SMS, remembers every ticket, and checks them against the real draw results — so a small win doesn't sit unnoticed until it expires. It works out every draw you paid to enter, scores each line, prices the wins, and flags what is still claimable and when it runs out. Everything stays on your own machine: no account, no API key, nothing paid. Specific to the South African National Lottery and, for now, Standard Bank's SMS wording.

screenshots.alt: Lotto Tracker's dark page, using invented tickets. Below a notice that one entry cannot be checked, it lists two winning lines, each with the ticket's numbers beside the numbers drawn as coloured balls, the prize amount and the date by which it can be claimed, then the tickets that still have draws to come.
A table of every ticket entry with its cost, how many draws were checked and what it won, followed by money spent against money won for the year.

Totals comparing what was spent with what was won, then the settings: a colour theme choice, switches for starting the tray at login and opening this page when the tray starts, and a Refresh results button.

projects.name: demoreel
projects.tagline: Record an app's demo video without filming your desktop.
projects.blurb: Records a short video of a desktop app running on a private virtual display — so nothing else you have open, and none of your accessibility tools, ends up in a file destined for a public pull request. One command takes an app and hands back a video file, optionally running a scripted list of clicks and keystrokes so the recording shows the app being used rather than sitting still. It refuses to return a blank recording: an empty display is an error, not a video.

video.caption: A silent 21-second clip of demoreel recording a demo of itself. In a dark terminal, the command 'demoreel record -o cube.mp4 -d 4 --gpu --app-log app.log -- vkcube' is typed and run. demoreel reports that it is recording private screen :3 for four seconds, then prints the finished video's path. That video is then played back below the terminal: a grey cube with teal LunarG logos, spinning. Nothing from the real desktop appears, because the terminal and the cube each ran on a private screen of their own.

projects.name: Local Web Server Manager
projects.tagline: See which of your local web servers are actually running.
projects.blurb: If you keep several web projects in one folder, each starts a different way, on a different port, and nothing tells you which are running. This scans your projects folder, works out how each one starts and which port it wants, and gives you a window with a row per project: a status light, a Start/Stop button, its live output and a link to open it. It runs each project's own start script and never edits your projects. Early days, but it runs: the window opens, the lights are live, and Start, Stop, Restart and Open work — driven from the keyboard if you prefer, with eight colour themes including two high-contrast ones. There is no download yet, so for now you run it from a copy of the source.

screenshots.alt: The Local Web Server Manager window in its dark Midnight theme, listing five sample web projects: Photo Gallery and Book Club are running, shown with green dots, Recipe Box and Budget Planner are stopped, and Weather Dashboard is unknown because it has no port. Each row has its port, a browser picker and Start, Stop, Restart and Open buttons.
The same five sample projects in the light Ledger theme, dark text on warm off-white, with the two running projects' Stop, Restart and Open buttons enabled.
The project list in the High contrast dark theme, white text with bright green and yellow status words on pure black, for readers who need the strongest contrast.
The word "book" typed into the filter box at the top narrows the list to the one matching project, Book Club, running on port 8604.

projects.name: Pressless
projects.tagline: Write and publish your own website from your own computer.
projects.blurb: A writing app that runs on your own machine and opens in your normal browser: you type an entry, see it exactly as it will look, and click once to publish it to your own free website — GitHub Pages today, with other hosts likely to follow. No accounts, no monthly fee and no service in between — every entry stays an ordinary text file in an ordinary folder, readable with Pressless closed, deleted or never installed. It is deliberately not a host: it never talks to your visitors and is not reachable from the internet. Writing, previewing and publishing work today; undo, photographs and a visitor dashboard are still to come.
